title: How a MOSFET Works: From Gate Voltage to Massive Current Flow

segments.label: Cold Open – The Invisible Switch
segments.text: What if a fingertip could blast a fire‑hose of electrons? That’s a MOSFET. A tiny gate voltage flips a massive drain‑source current, while the gate sips virtually no power. Think of a kitchen faucet: a light tap (the gate) unleashes a torrent through a huge pipe (the channel). How does a whisper of voltage pull that river? An electric field sneaks through an ultra‑thin oxide and summons an invisible conduction channel. The field acts like a magician’s wand, coaxing electrons to gather at the surface and form a bridge between source and drain. That bridge carries the load; the gate barely draws current. Did you ever wonder why your phone’s battery powers a bright screen with such a tiny control signal? Because the MOSFET’s gate draws almost zero steady‑state current. The first working MOSFET appeared in 1959, invented by Mohamed Atalla and Dawon Kahng at Bell Labs. The concept was first proposed by Julius Edgar Lilienfeld in 1925. When you apply voltage between gate and source, the field creates an inversion layer at the semiconductor‑oxide interface. segments.label: The MOS Structure – Gate, Oxide, and Body
segments.text: What sits between the gate and the silicon body? A thin slab of silicon‑dioxide, just a few nanometers thick. Think of it as the frosting on a cupcake: sweet, but it keeps the cake and the plate apart. The gate itself is metal or polysilicon, sitting on top of that frosting. Together they form a planar capacitor – one plate is the gate, the other is the semiconductor beneath the oxide. When you slap a voltage onto the gate, an electric field shoots through the oxide like a flashlight beam. It doesn’t stop at the frosting; it reaches the silicon surface and starts to rearrange charges there. How does that happen? The field pulls electrons toward the interface, pushing holes away, creating a region ready for conduction. This tiny stack, only a few atoms thick, is the heart of the MOSFET. It’s the same structure engineers have been perfecting since the late 1950s, using thermal oxidation to grow that oxide layer. Curious how that field actually creates a channel for current? Stay tuned, because next we’ll watch that inversion layer form and turn the switch on.

segments.label: Creating the Inversion Layer – From Depletion to Conduction
segments.text: Apply a positive gate‑to‑source voltage and the electric field pushes holes away from the oxide interface, leaving a thin depletion region of immobile, negatively charged acceptor ions. When the gate voltage exceeds the threshold (Vth), electrons are attracted to the surface, forming an inversion layer that converts the surface from p‑type to n‑type. This narrow n‑type channel links the heavily doped n+ source and drain, allowing electrons to flow freely under a drain‑to‑source voltage. Raising the gate voltage above Vth increases the electron density in the channel, so the current rises. Below Vth only a tiny subthreshold leakage flows. The MOSFET thus acts as a voltage‑controlled resistor, switching on when V_G > Vth and off otherwise. The first working MOSFET was built in 1959 by Mohamed Atalla and Dawon Kahng at Bell Labs, following Julius Edgar Lilienfeld’s 1925 field‑effect concept.

segments.label: Cutoff and Subthreshold – The ‘Off’ State
segments.text: What happens when you pull the gate voltage below the threshold? The MOSFET goes into cutoff. In cutoff, VGS < Vth, so the ideal model says no drain‑source current flows. But reality isn’t that perfect. Thermal energy kicks a few electrons over the energy barrier. Those lucky carriers create a tiny exponential subthreshold current: ID ≈ ID0 e^(VGS−Vth)/nVT. That equation comes straight from the Fermi‑Dirac distribution effect. Think of it like a leaky faucet – you can’t shut it off completely, a drip remains. Why does this matter? Because ultra‑low‑power circuits sometimes run right in that weak‑inversion region, exploiting the subthreshold leakage for analog functions. The leakage is tiny, but it’s measurable and follows the exponential rule. So even when you think the switch is off, a whisper of current still sneaks through. Curious how designers turn that whisper into a feature? They bias the gate just below Vth, letting the exponential law do the work. Stay tuned to see how the MOSFET behaves when you finally push the gate high enough to enter the triode, or linear, mode.

segments.label: Triode (Linear) Mode – Acting Like a Variable Resistor
segments.text: What happens when you keep the gate high enough to open the channel, but you don’t crank the drain voltage all the way? The MOSFET slips into triode mode. With VGS > Vth and VDS < VGS‑Vth, a conductive channel stretches from source to drain. Your drain‑to‑source current now follows ID = μn Cox (W/L) [(VGS‑Vth)VDS – VDS²/2]. Notice the first term grows linearly with VDS, while the second term is only a small correction. That means, for modest VDS, current rises almost proportionally to the drain voltage – just like a resistor. The gate voltage still sets the channel’s electron density, so you can tighten or loosen the “resistance” by nudging VGS. Think of it as turning a dimmer knob on a lamp: higher VGS makes the channel thicker, letting more current flow for the same VDS. Why does the current stop being perfectly linear as VDS grows? Because the VDS²/2 term starts to bite, curving the relationship. In practice, you treat the device as a voltage‑controlled resistor until VDS approaches VGS‑Vth, where saturation kicks in. Next, we’ll see what happens when you push the drain hard enough to force the channel to pinch off.

segments.label: Saturation (Active) Mode – The Switch Is Fully On
segments.text: When the gate voltage exceeds the threshold, an inversion layer forms and a channel bridges source and drain. Pulling the drain up squeezes the channel near the drain until it pinches off; the current then flattens and depends mainly on the gate voltage, not the drain voltage. This is the saturation region, where the MOSFET acts as a solid switch and a controlled current source. The device needs virtually no steady‑state input current, making it ideal for both digital switching and analog gain. The MOSFET—fabricated by controlled silicon oxidation with an insulated gate—was invented in 1959 by Mohamed Atalla and Dawon Kahng at Bell Labs, turning Julius Lilienfeld’s 1925 field‑effect concept into a practical component that powers modern electronics.
